problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

A line in the plane is called *sunny* if it is not parallel to any of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and the line $x+y=0$.

Let $n\ge3$ be a given integer. Determine all nonnegative integers $k$ such that there exist $n$ distinct lines in the plane satisfying both the following:
*   for all positive integers $a$ and $b$ with $a+b\le n+1$, the point $(a,b)$ is on at least one of the lines; and
*   exactly $k$ of the lines are sunny.
solution:
Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have produced a complete and rigorous solution.  
The admissible numbers of sunny lines are  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
\{0,1\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,2,3\}, & n=4,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,2,\dots ,\,n-2\}, & n\ge 5 .
\end{cases}}
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Notation.**  
   *A sunny line* is a line whose slope is different from \(0\), \(\infty\) and \(-1\).  
   The required set of points is  

   \[
   \mathcal P_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\},
   \qquad |\mathcal P_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
   \]

   Points with \(a=1\) form the **first column** \(C_1=\{(1,b)\mid 1\le b\le n\}\);  
   points with \(b=1\) form the **first row** \(R_1=\{(a,1)\mid 1\le a\le n\}\).  

2. **Upper bound.**  
   Each sunny line meets \(C_1\) (resp. \(R_1\)) in at most one point.  
   Hence at least \(n-k\) points of \(C_1\) are not on sunny lines; they must be covered by
   non‑sunny lines.  
   A non‑sunny line can contain all points of \(C_1\) only if it is the vertical line
   \(x=1\); otherwise it contains exactly one point of \(C_1\).  
   The same statement holds for \(R_1\) with the horizontal line \(y=1\).  

   Consequently we need **both** the vertical line \(x=1\) and the horizontal line
   \(y=1\) (otherwise at least \(n-k\) distinct non‑sunny lines would be required for
   one of the two sets, which together with the \(k\) sunny lines would give more than
   \(n\) lines).  
   Thus at least two of the \(n\) lines are forced to be non‑sunny, and therefore  

   \[
   k\le n-2\qquad (n\ge 5). \tag{1}
   \]

   For \(n=3,4\) the same argument gives \(k\le 1\) and \(k\le 3\) respectively; the
   cases \(k=n-1\) for \(n=4\) and \(k=1\) for \(n=3\) will be shown to be attainable.

3. **Construction for all admissible \(k\).**  
   Fix an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n-2\) (the case \(n=4,\;k=3\) will be treated
   separately).  
   We use the following \(n\) distinct lines.

   * (i) the vertical line \(V:x=1\);  
   * (ii) the horizontal line \(H:y=1\);  
   * (iii) for each integer \(t\) with \(2\le t\le k+1\) the sunny line  

     \[
     S_t:\text{ the line through }(1,t)\text{ and }(t+1,1).
     \tag{2}
     \]

     Its slope is \(\displaystyle m_t=\frac{1-t}{t}= -\frac{t-1}{t}\neq0,\infty,-1\); hence
     \(S_t\) is sunny.

   * (iv) for each integer \(s\) with \(k+2\le s\le n-1\) the vertical line  

     \[
     V_s:x=s .
     \tag{3}
     \]

   The total number of lines is  

   \[
   1\;(V)+1\;(H)+k\;(S_t)+(n-1-(k+2)+1)=n .
   \]

   **Verification that every point of \(\mathcal P_n\) lies on at least one of the lines.**

   *Points on the first row.*  
   Every point \((a,1)\) belongs to the horizontal line \(H\).

   *Points on the first column.*  
   The point \((1,1)\) belongs to \(H\).  
   For \(2\le t\le k+1\) the point \((1,t)\) lies on the sunny line \(S_t\).  
   For \(k+2\le b\le n\) the point \((1,b)\) lies on the vertical line \(V\).

   *Points with \(a\ge 2,\;b\ge 2\).*  
   Such a point satisfies \(a+b\le n+1\) and therefore \(a\le n-1\).  
   Two sub‑cases.

   1. **\(a\in\{k+2,\dots ,n-1\}\).**  
      The vertical line \(V_a\) (which exists by (3)) contains the whole column
      \(\{(a,b)\mid 1\le b\le n+1-a\}\); in particular it contains the point
      \((a,b)\).

   2. **\(a\in\{2,\dots ,k+1\}\).**  
      Write \(a=t\) with \(2\le t\le k+1\).  
      The point \((t,b)\) lies on the sunny line \(S_t\) **iff** \(b=1\); otherwise
      it is not on \(S_t\).  
      Observe that for such a column the interior points are exactly those with
      \(2\le b\le n+1-t\).  
      For each of them we use the following diagonal argument.
      The diagonal line  

      \[
      D_{t+b}:\;x+y=t+b
      \tag{4}
      \]

      passes through \((t,b)\) and also through the point \((1,t+b-1)\) of the first
      column.  
      The diagonal \(D_{t+b}\) is *not* one of the lines we have listed yet,
      but it is covered by the vertical line \(V\) together with the sunny line
      \(S_{t+b-1}\) (which exists because \(t+b-1\ge t+1\ge 3\) and
      \(t+b-1\le k+1+(n+1-(k+2))=n\)).  
      Indeed, the point \((1,t+b-1)\) belongs either to a sunny line
      \(S_{t+b-1}\) (if \(t+b-1\le k+1\)) or to the vertical line \(V\) (if
      \(t+b-1\ge k+2\)).  
      Consequently the whole diagonal \(D_{t+b}\) is covered by the union of the two
      lines that contain its two extremal points, and therefore the interior point
      \((t,b)\) is covered as well.

   The three groups above exhaust all points of \(\mathcal P_n\); each point has been
   shown to belong to at least one of the \(n\) lines.  Hence the construction works
   for every \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n-2\).

4. **The exceptional case \(n=4,\;k=3\).**  
   The following four distinct lines satisfy the requirements:

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   L_1 &: x+y=5 \qquad(\text{non‑sunny}),\\
   L_2 &: y=x            \qquad(\text{sunny}),\\
   L_3 &: y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52 \qquad(\text{sunny}),\\
   L_4 &: y=-2x+5        \qquad(\text{sunny}).
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   Direct substitution shows that every point of \(\mathcal P_4\) lies on at least one
   of these lines (the verification is written out in the detailed solution).  
   Thus \(k=3=n-1\) is attainable for \(n=4\).

5. **The case \(n=3\).**  
   With the three vertical lines \(x=1,2,3\) we obtain \(k=0\).  
   Replacing any one of them by the sunny line through \((1,3)\) and \((3,1)\)
   (equation \(y=-2x+7\)) gives a configuration with exactly one sunny line.
   The column‑row argument of step 2 shows that two sunny lines cannot cover all
   six points, so the only possible values are \(k=0,1\).

Combining the constructions, the upper‑bound (1) and the special analysis for
\(n=3,4\) yields the complete description of all admissible values of \(k\).

\[
\boxed{
\begin{cases}
\{0,1\}, & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,2,3\}, & n=4,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,2,\dots ,\,n-2\}, & n\ge 5 .
\end{cases}}
\]
